steps.observation: Work on this for 900 seconds; do not stop early. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here’s a concise overview of the key structural and functional differences between DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid):

1. Sugar backbone  
  • DNA contains deoxyribose, which lacks an –OH group on the 2′ carbon.  
  • RNA contains ribose, which has an –OH group on both the 2′ and 3′ carbons.  
  • The extra 2′-OH in RNA makes it more chemically reactive (and less stable) than DNA.

2. Nitrogenous bases  
  • DNA uses adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T).  
  • RNA uses A, G, C and uracil (U) in place of thymine.  
  • Uracil pairs with adenine via two hydrogen bonds, just like T–A in DNA.

3. Strand architecture  
  • DNA is most often double-stranded, forming the familiar right-handed double helix.  
  • RNA is usually single-stranded, though it can fold back on itself into complex secondary structures (hairpins, loops, bulges).

4. Function  
  • DNA: long-term storage of genetic information in the nucleus (eukaryotes) or nucleoid (prokaryotes).  
  • RNA: diverse roles in decoding, regulation and expression of that information. Major classes include  
     – mRNA (messenger RNA): carries coding instructions from DNA to ribosomes  
     – tRNA (transfer RNA): brings amino acids to ribosomes during protein synthesis  
     – rRNA (ribosomal RNA): structural and catalytic component of ribosomes  
     – Other regulatory and catalytic RNAs (e.g. miRNA, siRNA, ribozymes)

5. Stability and lifespan  
  • DNA is highly stable under cellular conditions; it can persist for the life of the cell or organism.  
  • RNA is relatively short-lived, which suits its roles in rapid transcriptional regulation and protein synthesis.

6. Cellular location  
  • In eukaryotes, DNA resides primarily in the nucleus (and also in mitochondria/chloroplasts).  
  • RNA is synthesized in the nucleus but functions throughout the cytoplasm (and in organelles).

In sum, DNA’s chemically stable, double-stranded structure makes it ideal for long-term genetic storage, whereas RNA’s single-stranded, versatile nature enables it to act as the primary “working copy” and regulator of genetic information.
